original_question: For semi-algebraic sets, are the middle Betti numbers intrinsically harder to compute than the lowest and highest Betti numbers or the Euler-Poincare characteristic? In particular, is there a complexity-theoretic hardness result that explains the apparent algorithmic gap, or an analogue of the phenomenon from smooth projective complex varieties in which the middle Betti numbers contain essentially all the information?

correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper's exact target: it is about semi-algebraic sets, it contrasts the middle Betti numbers with the lowest and highest Betti numbers and with the Euler-Poincare characteristic, and it asks for a complexity-theoretic hardness explanation together with the analogy to smooth projective complex varieties. This matches the wording of the Section 9 open problem almost verbatim. ([math.purdue.edu](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~sbasu/ams_final_submission.pdf))
missing_details: The paper states this as an open problem, not as a theorem, conjecture, or established hardness result.
The ambient setting is semi-algebraic sets S ⊂ R^k over a real closed field R; this is the paper's standing notation.
Betti numbers are cohomological Betti numbers with Q-coefficients: for closed and bounded S, b_i(S) = dim_Q H^i(S).
For closed but not necessarily bounded S, the survey defines H^i(S) as H^i(S ∩ B_k(0,r)) for all sufficiently large r > 0, using local conic structure at infinity.

For locally closed semi-algebraic sets, the Euler-Poincare characteristic in the survey is the Borel-Moore Euler-Poincare characteristic χ_BM(S) = Σ_i (-1)^i b_i^BM(S), defined from (S_r, overline(S_r) \ S_r) for sufficiently large r; for closed and bounded sets this agrees with the ordinary χ(S).
The paper does not formally define a specific index range for "middle"; it uses the term informally to mean Betti numbers away from the bottom and top ends.

No degree restriction, homogeneity assumption, or quadratic-input restriction is part of the formal open problem itself; those belong only to the motivating algorithmic evidence discussed earlier in the survey.

The algorithmic asymmetry motivating the question is that the first few Betti numbers admit single-exponential algorithms in general, the top few Betti numbers admit polynomial-time algorithms in the quadratic case, and the Euler-Poincare characteristic is also easier in the quadratic case.
refined_question: Let R be a real closed field and let S ⊂ R^k be a semi-algebraic set. Writing b_i(S) for the i-th Betti number of S with Q-coefficients in the sense of the survey (for closed and bounded S, b_i(S) = dim_Q H^i(S)), is there a complexity-theoretic explanation for the apparent algorithmic asymmetry that the low Betti numbers, the top Betti numbers, and the Euler-Poincare characteristic of semi-algebraic sets seem easier to compute than the intermediate ("middle") Betti numbers? More specifically, can one prove a hardness result, or formulate a complexity-theoretic analogue of the smooth projective complex variety phenomenon, showing that the middle Betti numbers essentially carry the difficult topological information? ([math.purdue.edu](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~sbasu/ams_final_submission.pdf))
justification: The nearest official formulation is the unnumbered Section 9 open problem itself, whose wording your draft already tracks closely. The nearby context that makes the question precise is the survey's standing notation for semi-algebraic sets over a real closed field, its definition of Betti numbers and Euler-Poincare characteristic, and the earlier algorithmic results that motivate the asymmetry: single-exponential algorithms for the first few Betti numbers in general (Theorem 6.10), polynomial-time algorithms for the top Betti numbers in the quadratic case (Theorem 7.22), efficient computation of Euler-Poincare characteristic in the quadratic case (Theorem 7.9), and an earlier #P-hardness statement for certain low-index Betti numbers for basic sets defined by quadratic inequalities. ([math.purdue.edu](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~sbasu/ams_final_submission.pdf))
